html:
The Achaean League was a federation of Greek cities in the northern Peloponnese, refounded around 280 BCE, which for a time united most of the Peloponnese until Rome broke it up in 146 BCE.

Achaea, the strip of land along the Gulf of Corinth, had an older league of small cities in classical times; one of its leading members, Helike, was swallowed by the sea in 373 BCE. In the 200s BCE the league was rebuilt as a true federal state, with shared citizenship, a common army, coins, weights and an elected general. Under Aratus of Sicyon it grew to take in Corinth, Argos and Megalopolis.

Its rival was Sparta. When the reforming Spartan king Cleomenes III threatened it, Aratus called in his old enemy, Macedon. King Antigonus III Doson came with an army, set up the Hellenic League, and beat Cleomenes at the Battle of Sellasia in 222 BCE. Later, under Philopoemen, the league absorbed Sparta itself.

It sided with Rome against Macedon, but Rome distrusted it. After the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE, a thousand leading Achaeans were taken to Italy as hostages, among them the historian Polybius, who explained the league's ideals in his history. In 146 BCE the league went to war with Rome and lost; the consul Mummius sacked Corinth, and Greece came under Roman control.
sum: The Achaean League was a federation of Greek cities in the northern Peloponnese, refounded around 280 BCE, which for a time united most of the Peloponnese until Rome broke it up in 146 BCE.
